newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists protest against retroactivity of law.
newsitem.headline: HK activists protest against retroactivity of law.

text.p: A group of Hong Kong democracy activists protested on Monday against the future government's plans to bring in retroactive laws after the territory reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
"Criminal prosecutions should not be retroactive," a dozen or so protesters chanted in front of the glassy tower block where future leader Tung Chee-hwa has his office.
"We protest against the future Justice Secretary ignoring the rule of law and suppressing demonstrations," one said.

On Saturday, future Justice Secretary Elsie Leung warned democracy activists against defying post-handover laws governing protests in the hours between the midnight handover and the passage of a bill putting the laws into effect a few hours later, early on July 1.

Leung said there would be no legal vacuum as the bills would be made retroactive to midnight on June 30, and she would consider prosecuting any unlawful demonstration staged shortly after the change of rule.
If anyone tried to make use of those few hours to act against the laws, she would use her discretion in deciding whether or not to prosecute them, she said.
The laws to be confirmed include a provision requiring organisers of demonstrations to obtain prior police permission.
"We criticise...this ridiculous statement because that's contradictory to Common Law practice," said Andrew Cheng, one of the protesters.
The British Common Law, which will stay effective under a Sino-British treaty governing the change of rule, does not allow new criminal laws to be retroactive, Cheung noted.
Protesters said retroactivity violated provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights which is applicable to Hong Kong.
"The International Covenant of Civil and Political Rights clearly states that any criminal sanction must not have a retrospective effect," Cheng said.

"Ms Leung's comments clearly challenged the spirit and regulation of the Common Law, and cast doubts over the future judiciary system," the protesters said in a statement. The legal grounds behind Leung's statement were doubtful, it said.
Cheung said Leung's comments had aroused worries that the move would set a precedent of retroactivity and was aimed at suppressing freedom.
Protesters demanded an apology and a withdrawal of Leung's statement, which they said was aimed at banning demonstrations.

The demonstrators were members of The United Front Against the Provisional Legislature, angry at China's decision to scrap Hong Kong's fully-elected legislature and install the appointed interim chamber in its place.
The Front plans to stage a protest against the provisional body in the early hours of July 1 -- before it can sit and pass the bill confirming the new laws.
Andrew To, one of the protesters, said the group had notified the police about the plan but did not intend to seek permission.
On Monday, meanwhile, the colonial government dropped charges against 13 group members charged with violating frontier restrictions during a December protest over the new interim assembly, To said.
In return for seeing the charges dropped, the activists agreed to be bound over for 12 months, he added.
